tip: 'Lebih' + adjective + 'daripada' compares: 'lebih sejuk daripada di Jakarta' = cooler than in Jakarta.
'Musim' = season. Indonesia has two: 'musim hujan' (rainy) and 'musim kemarau' (dry).
The 'ke-…-an' wrapper around a noun = affected by it: 'kehujanan' = caught in the rain.
Doubling a verb relaxes it: 'jalan-jalan' = to stroll, go out (not just 'walk').
No perfect tense needed – 'sudah' plus a time span covers 'has been': 'Sudah tiga hari hujan tidak berhenti' = it's been three days of nonstop rain.
'Kata' + source = 'according to': 'kata ramalan cuaca' = according to the weather forecast.
'Dulu' after a command = 'for now / yet': 'jangan jemur pakaian dulu' = don't hang the laundry out yet.
'Tidak apa-apa' is literally 'not anything' – doubling 'apa' (what) turns it into 'anything', so the whole phrase means 'it's nothing, no problem'.
'Jadi' before an adjective = 'becomes': 'udara jadi sejuk' = the air turns cool.
Doubled 'mana' = 'everywhere': 'ke mana-mana' (to everywhere), 'di mana-mana' (everywhere).
The prefix 'se-' before a noun can mean one whole unit: 'sekeluarga' = the whole family, 'sekelas' = the whole class.
'Yang' links a question word to its verb: 'Musik apa yang biasanya kamu dengarkan?' = what music do you usually listen to?
Doubling a verb makes it leisurely: 'jalan' = walk, 'jalan-jalan' = stroll around for fun. It's not walking twice – it's the casual version.
Doubling an adjective spreads it over many items: 'bagus-bagus' = all (of them) good.
'Paling' = 'the most' and never changes the word after it: 'paling kamu suka' = you like the most. English swaps to -est or 'most'; Indonesian just drops in 'paling'.
'Baru' before a verb = just (recently): 'baru mulai' = just started.
In conversation the 'meN-' prefix often drops: 'memasak' → 'masak', 'mencuci' → 'cuci'.
'Jumat malam' = Friday night; 'malam Jumat' means Thursday night (the eve of Friday).
'Bukan' negates nouns, 'tidak' negates verbs: 'bukan hobi saya' = not my hobby.
'Depan' after a time word = next: 'akhir pekan depan' = next weekend, 'bulan depan' = next month.
'Itu' here isn't 'that' – it marks where a long subject ends: 'bermain game di ponsel itu' = as for playing phone games. No word for 'is' needed after.
Order decides the meaning: 'jam tujuh' = seven o'clock, but 'tujuh jam' = seven hours. 'Jam' first reads the clock; the number first counts a duration.
'Nanti' = later, usually the same day: 'nanti malam' = tonight; 'nanti sore' = later this afternoon.
'Ketemu' is the everyday spoken form of 'bertemu': 'ketemu jam lima' = meet at five.
'Tidak jadi' = (a plan) falls through: 'Piknik tidak jadi' = the picnic is off.
'Janji' = promise or appointment: 'ada janji' = to have an appointment.
'Jadi' checks a plan is still on: 'jadi pergi?' = are we still going?
Word order flips the meaning: 'jam dua' = two o'clock, but 'dua jam' = two hours. Here 'janji kita jam dua' = our appointment at two.
'Tadi' = earlier, in the recent past: 'tadi malam' = last night. It pairs with 'nanti' – 'nanti' looks ahead, 'tadi' looks back.
The suffix '-nya' can mean 'the': 'hotelnya' = the hotel; 'kuncinya' = the key.
